blocks.text: The pituitary gland hangs from the hypothalamus by a stalk, the infundibulum, and has three lobes: anterior, posterior and intermediate (median).

blocks.caption: Hormones of the pituitary
rows: growth of muscles, bones (indirectly) and other tissues; needed for proper metabolism
makes the adrenal cortex secrete corticosteroids, which regulate glucose and salt balance
makes the thyroid produce thyroxine, which stimulates oxidative respiration
females: ovaries produce progesterone and estrogen, ovulation; males: testes produce testosterone
females: development of ovarian follicles; males: development of sperm (FSH and LH are gonadotropins)
mammary glands produce milk; made in both sexes, works only in females
milk ejection (contraction of smooth muscle of the mammary glands); uterine contractions in childbirth
melanocytes of skin and hair make and release melanin

blocks.text: The posterior pituitary does not make hormones: it contains axons from the hypothalamus and only stores and releases hormones made there. It forms in the embryo as an outgrowth of neural tissue, which is why it stays joined to the hypothalamus by a tract of axons. In breast-feeding mothers oxytocin secretion continues after birth, so the uterus returns to its normal size sooner.

blocks.alt: The hypothalamus with its stalk and the two pituitary lobes, with blood vessels to the anterior lobe and axons of the hypothalamus to the posterior lobe. Green arrows from the anterior pituitary: TSH to the thyroid, ACTH to the adrenal cortex, FSH and LH to the ovary and to the testis, GH to bones and skeletal muscles, prolactin to the mammary glands. Red arrows from the posterior pituitary: oxytocin to the mammary glands and the uterus, ADH to the kidney.
blocks.caption: Figure 16.3: Hormones of anterior & posterior pituitary and their target sites (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 16.3; every anterior-lobe arrow drawn from the anterior lobe).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 16.3 draws the GH and prolactin arrows from beneath the posterior lobe; both are hormones of the anterior pituitary, so the drawing above takes them from the anterior lobe.

items: Too much GH in a growing child: gigantism, height well above average with enlarged hands, feet and face. Too much GH in adults: acromegaly, bones thicken but cannot lengthen, so the hands, feet, skull, nose and jaw enlarge.
Too little GH: dwarfism, slow development and short stature, but the body stays in proportion and brain development and IQ are unaffected.
Too much TSH: hyperthyroidism (excess thyroxine); too little: hypothyroidism (lack of thyroxine).
Too little ADH: diabetes insipidus, a large output of dilute urine and frequent thirst; too much ADH may lead to kidney problems.
Too much oxytocin may rupture the uterine wall; too little hinders normal labour.

blocks.title: Growth hormone treatment
blocks.text: GH is given to children who are short because of GH deficiency, and it improves their growth rate. Not every short person lacks GH, so the treatment is not right for everyone, and doctors do not support using GH to build muscle or slow ageing.
